ev.text: Stress in Yale seems to be primarily sonority-driven. The basic stress assignment algorithm seems to be something like the following. (19) 1. Mark the last syllable as extrametrical. 2. Assign primary stress to a penultimate /a/. 3. If there is none, assign stress to an antipenultimate /a/. 4. If there is none, run the above two steps with /ɛ/ instead. 5. Make the primary stressed syllable the head of a foot, and make feet around it as space allows. Feet can be iambic or trochaic; the choice is determined by which allows the maximum number of footed syllables. ... However, the majority of Yale words seem to have no noticeable stress at all

All monosyllabic words (as the entire word is extrametrical), and all disyllabic words (as the only possible foot is degenerate, which Yale doesn't seem to allow)'; the stress algorithm (19) operates on the word ('Mark the last syllable as extrametrical'), and utterance-level pitch is treated separately…

5072.heavy: Not syllable weight. 2020: stress attracted by vowel sonority, /a/ outranking /ɛ/ and other vowels never attracting stress; fn. 9 p. 24: 'This does not seem to point towards syllable weight influencing stress placement—all unexpected stress placements involve falling pitch.' Contour (falling) pitch on the penult attracts stress regardless of vowel. OPD: 'very short syllables are not counted in the stress placement' (p. 3), i.e. extra-short syllables are invisible to the penult count.
5072.dflt: 2020: no stress at all ('Words with no non-final /a/ or /ɛ/' are stressless, p. 24); OPD: n/a (penultimate is the default position)
5072.prule: Two first-hand descriptions of the same field data disagree on the architecture. Campbell & Campbell 2001 (the fieldworkers' phonology sheet): stress is word-level, mostly penultimate ('the greatest majority of two syllable words are stressed on the penultimate'; 3+ syllable words penult or antepenult), 'assigned in the lexicon and not purely assigned by rules', 'appears to be contrastive' (five minimal pairs, e.g. 'so.lo 'fish net' vs so.'lo 'sip'), with very short syllables not counted; no tone mentioned. Aannestad 2020 (reanalysis of the Campbells' archived tapes, no fieldwork): tone is phonemic ('It seems clear that tone is phonemic', p. 21), 'stress is dependent on tone (and vowel quality)' (p. 20), and stress is 'primarily sonority-driven': final syllable extrametrical; primary stress to a penultimate /a/, else an antepenultimate /a/, else the same with /ɛ/; feet built around it iambic or trochaic; 'the majority of Yale words seem to have no noticeable stress at all', including all monosyllables and all disyllables (p. 24). The OPD's stressed, contrastive disyllables are thus stressless tonal contrasts under the 2020 analysis; neither source discusses the other's stress claim, both hedge ('we think', 'seems').
5072.srule: Aannestad, Campbell & Campbell 2020 only, tentative: the primary-stressed syllable heads a binary foot and further feet are built around it as space allows (final syllable extrametrical, no degenerate feet), iambic or trochaic, whichever foots the most syllables; the head of an additional foot bears secondary stress, e.g. walugaluju 'mouth harp' -> (ˌwalu)(ˈgalu)ju, secondary two syllables before the primary. Most words, including all mono- and disyllables, have no stress at all (p. 24). Campbell & Campbell 2001 OPD: secondary stress not mentioned ('Suprasegmentals', p. 3).

However, if such a hierarchy is truly the case, this paper can say little to nothing definitive about prosody in Yale'. The OPD's section is headed 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' but says nothing about tone.

5072.cfw: The only two descriptions of Yale, both built on the Campbells' own field data, disagree on what kind of system the language has: Campbell & Campbell 2001 describe lexically assigned, contrastive stress that is mostly penultimate and say nothing about tone, while Aannestad, Campbell & Campbell 2020 treat Yale as tonal, derive stress from vowel sonority (a penultimate or antepenultimate /a/, else /ɛ/, the final syllable never stressed) and call most words, every disyllable included, stressless, and no third description exists to settle it.

5073.dq: Primary stress in Yaminawa is word-initial. Metrical feet are left-aligned and iteratively trochaic, with no degenerate feet.
5073.dloc: Appendix C, §C.4.2 'Stress', pp. 257-258; tone/stress independence §C.4.5 'Tone', pp. 273-274 and §C.4 intro; variety identity §2.2.
5073.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word, regardless of syllable weight (a closed non-initial syllable does not attract it, ex. 117f; long vowels occur only word-initially, so the author notes their effect cannot be tested); cued by vowel duration (about 10-20 percent longer).
5073.srule: Secondary stress on every odd-numbered non-initial syllable (3rd, 5th, 7th...): left-aligned iterative syllabic trochees, no degenerate feet (a final odd syllable is unstressed), weight-insensitive; e.g. (ˈá.wá)(ˌwɨ̀.dà) 'butterfly', (ˈɨ́.kɨ̀ʂ)(ˌtì.ɾù)wù 'they may sew', (ˈw̃ɨ.nã)(ˌmã.ɾìʃ)(ˌtá.kũ)ĩ. Impressionistic exception: verbs with trisyllabic reduplicants put secondary stress on the 4th syllable (first syllable of the verbal stem), (119) (ˈbɨ́.tʃú)kù(ˌbɨ́.tʃú)(ˌkù.bɨ̀)j.

5073.tone: Yaminawa also has lexical tone: TBU = syllable, underlying melodies H, L, HL, underspecified syllables surface L (§C.4.5, p. 273-274). The author states 'There is no evidence for interactions between tone and stress.' (p. 274) and 'The tone and stress systems do not appear to interact.' (§C.4). Faust & Loos 2002 (SLP 51, p. 18) conflate the two ('acento y tono alto'): transitive verb roots carry accent/high tone on the first two syllables, intransitive roots on the first only, 'La primera sílaba de la frase nominal es tónica' -- initial prominence agrees with Neely; Neely's analysis puts the transitive/intransitive difference in tone, not stress.

Consistent with §2.1.4 (p. 880): 'В структурах типа CVLV обычно происходит редукция первого гласного, порой до полного его исчезновения, особенно в быстрой речи' (the first vowel of a CVLV foot is usually reduced, sometimes to zero, especially in fast speech). Nothing is stated for words of several feet (a word is at least one foot, §2.5.0 p. 894).

5082.dflt: first syllable of the word (disyllables with open second syllable, trisyllabic monomorphemes, inflected final verbs and Medial verbs without Different Subject marking); penultimate in a listed set of trisyllables; unpredictable in 4-5 syllable monomorphemes
5082.prule: One primary stress per phonological word; stress non-contrastive. Default first-syllable stress (disyllables with open second syllable 'almost always'; trisyllabic monomorphemes 'usually'; inflected final verbs 'usually'). Heavy syllables attract stress: closed syllables, long vowels and diphthongs, and weakly the vowel /u/ — in (C)V.CVC disyllables 'most' have final stress (with 'quite a few exceptions', Table 2.8); long vowels 'usually stressed' (p. 2); diphthongs created by verbal suffixation take the stress (ongo-i [ɔˈŋɔɪ], iso-un-a [iˈsɔu.na]); monosyllabic V-final verb root + /u/-nucleus suffix (-nung, -gu-ng) stressed finally. Four- and five-syllable monomorphemes: 'stress is unpredictable'. Verbs and non-verbs follow different systems; stress in verbs is 'predictable', in nouns 'not entirely predictable' (p. 66).
5082.srule: Secondary stress is placed by verbal morphology: Near Future inflections carry a secondary stress on -ka-, the first element of the historical auxiliary (dawi-wang-ka-t [ˈda.βi.waŋˌkhat˺]); in past Habitual Dependent verb=it- 'be' fusions the inflected auxiliary bears only secondary stress, with primary stress on the first syllable of the lexical root ([ˈɔng.ɔng.itːˌduŋ]); the Completive enclitic =dup bears secondary stress. No general or rhythmic secondary-stress rule is stated for other words; secondary marks otherwise appear only in transcriptions (Hesienare [ˌhɛ.si.jɛˈna.rɛ], nimbuharak-ni [ˌni.mbu.haˈrak.ni], humbor-un-a [ˈhu.mbɔˌru.na]).

5083.tone: Kamholz analyses Yaur as a lexical tone language (H vs L per mora) with contrastive vowel length and posits no stress. Everything the sources say about stress: (a) 2017 p. 9 fn. 3 hedges that some of what he analyses as length or tone 'could be reanalyzed as stress (more plausible in some cases than others)', without proposing any stress analysis; (b) 2017 p. 8 counts Yaur among the six SHWNG languages 'known to be tonal' (own fieldwork); (c) 2014 diss. p. 117: 'Traces of former penultimate stress were found in Ma'ya, Moor, and Yerisiam' and penultimate stress is 'cited as the regular or default pattern' in Buli, Sawai, Taba, Ambai, Wandamen, Waropen, Warembori -- Yaur is in neither list; (d) 2017 Table 17 p. 28 summarises Yaur's tonal innovations as 'No robust generalizations'. No synchronic stress position, weight rule or accent placement is stated for Yaur anywhere in either work.

tn.translation: Like other Zapotec languages, zsby is a tonal language. It contrasts three tones: high, low and rising. It also has two types of laryngealization: mid-anchored and final-anchored. ... In all these two- or three-syllable words, stress always falls on the last one ... The acoustic correlates of stress involve greater duration and a more defined formant structure in the vowels ... Pitch or F0 is not an acoustic correlate of stress in zsby, since this is a tonal language and F0 is used mainly to make tonal distinctions.

5085.heavy: Not weight-sensitive: 'la longitud vocálica y las variaciones de tono lo acompañan, careciendo de autonomía fonémica' (length and pitch are non-phonemic concomitants of the stress).
5085.prule: Stress ('acento de intensidad') is phonemic and contrastive: the language is not tonal, vowel length and pitch only accompany stress without phonemic autonomy; the single word stress falls almost always on the first or the second syllable of the word regardless of the word's total syllable count, and its position is lexical, as minimal pairs with initial vs. second-syllable stress show (wíjla 'peinar' vs. wijlá 'flecha de cerbatana'; kájate 'cazabe' vs. kajáte 'frío'; jlíjani 'hijo' vs. jlijáni 'garrapata pequeña'). A small listed set of words carries third-syllable stress (wakuláya, walipópo...; terekáyu, morokóto are called unassimilated loans). Morphology interacts: adding the possessive suffix -ne (or any other possessive suffix) shifts the word stress one syllable to the left, unless it is already on the first syllable, in which case it stays (síja 'piedra' > síjane; mayúlu 'cuenta de collar' > máyulune; yáju 'espejo' > yájune).

5086.heavy: Primary stress: none; the source says stress goes to the first syllable 'regardless of the number of syllables or moras that make up the word'. Secondary stress only (p. 98): 'Mora counting in this language is based on the number of sonorant (including vocalic) segments in words. Non-syllabic sonorants (nasals, liquids and approximants) that occur in a preconsonantal environment (i.e. as an off-set C2 segment of a medial C1VC2 syllable) are counted as constituting one mora. Word-final sonorants are not considered as constituting a mora.' Obstruent codas and vowel length add no mora.
5086.dflt: not applicable (primary stress is initial regardless of syllable weight, in over 98% of words; the mora count only positions secondary stress)
5086.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word, regardless of the number of syllables or moras (quantity-insensitive, count-blind): 1704 of 1730 nominals (over 98%) in Hosokawa's dictionary count, and always word-initial (on the first-order prefix) in conjugated verbs.
5086.srule: One secondary stress per word, placed by mora count from the word start (mora = each vowel plus each preconsonantal sonorant coda of a medial syllable; word-final sonorants, obstruent codas and vowel length add none): on the 3rd mora if it is a vowel, otherwise on the 4th-mora vowel unless that vowel is word-final, in which case none (Table 314: cv'.cv.cv` dyanadya, cv'.s.cv` dyimbu, cv'.cv.cv`.cv wanangarri, but cv'.cv.s.cv kardimba with no secondary). In polymorphemic words morphology overrides the count: first syllable of the (first) suffix, of the non-initial compound member and of the reduplicant, and the root-initial syllable in conjugated verbs.

5088.dq: The domain of primary stress is the phonological word. All clitics are lexically stressed and do not affect the assignment of primary stress
5088.dloc: p. 111 (introduction: two degrees of stress, heavy = final consonant or long vowel, primary = rightmost stress); p. 112 sec. 1 (domain), sec. 1.1 Verbal Stress, sec. 1.2 Nominal Stress; p. 113 coronal-obstruent codas light, examples (4)-(6); p. 114 rules (7)-(8) and exceptions (9); p. 115 exceptions (10)-(11) and sec. 1.3 Exceptions to verb stress assignment; pp. 127-128 generalisation (65).
5088.heavy: Heavy syllables are defined as having either a final consonant or a long vowel nucleus (p. 111); for noun primary stress a word-final syllable closed by a coronal obstruent [-son, +cor] is considered light and not stressed, a final syllable closed by any other segment is heavy and stressed, and a final syllable with a long vowel is heavy even if closed by a coronal obstruent (p. 113); a word-final syllable ending in /n/ is always stressed (p. 127).
5088.dflt: penult (nouns with a light final syllable, e.g. [stápu] 'beans', [múkskut] 'fever'); verbs: ultima regardless of weight (or penult when a word-final inflectional suffix is extrametrical)
5088.prule: Nouns: primary stress on the final syllable if it is heavy (long vowel, or closed by any consonant other than a coronal obstruent), otherwise on the penult; word-final CV and CVC-with-coronal-obstruent-coda syllables are light/extrametrical. Secondary stress on every heavy syllable (CVC or CVV); primary stress = the rightmost stress in the phonological word. MacKay's formulation (7)-(8), p. 114: final light syllables extrametrical; build right-dominant quantity-sensitive feet; right-dominant word tree.
5088.srule: Secondary stress on every heavy syllable (closed syllable or long vowel: CVC, CVV); primary stress is the right-most of these stresses; a light CV syllable never bears secondary stress; predictable, so unmarked in MacKay's transcriptions. (MacKay 1994 sec. 6, per archive.org excerpt, additionally puts secondary stress on 'the first syllable of a word'; MacKay 1999 p. 73 and MacKay & Trechsel 2005 again say heavy syllables only.)

5089.prule: Word stress ('accent dynamique', marked by a dot only where it deviates) falls almost always on the first syllable of the word; fixed initial, quantity-insensitive, stated independently of the three-way tonal accent system.

5089.tone: Tone language. Strub (p. 452 §4): three 'accents toniques' — high (´), low (`), rising (ˇ) — plus unmarked mid; tone is 'indispensable' and he gives minimal sets (akpa 'oiseau de proie' / akpà 'coupe à boire' / ákpà 'banne'; ọ́bọ̀ 'main' / ọ́bọ 'chef; prêtre' / ọbọ̀ 'sacrifice' / ọ́bo 'jamais' as read, diacritics approximate) and a musical-notation table of the intervals. Modern descriptions treat the language as purely tonal and say nothing about stress: Laver 1967 (Aviele dialect; four tones: high, low, high-fall, downstep; the scan, no 'stress/accent' hit) and Elimelech 1976 = 1978 (Ekpheli dialect; two underlying tones, five surface pitches, downdrift/downstep; the scan of Ch. I-III and bibliography, no 'stress/accent/prominence' hit). Strub's 'accent dynamique' is a separate, explicitly non-tonal prominence.

tn.translation: In Dida, each syllable, simple or complex, can bear only one tone. ... The tonology of Dida shows the following characteristics: a) Dida has three register tones, attested in the following realisations: [su] H 'push' [su] M 'tree' [su] B 'be excited' b) Dida has no contour (modulated) tones. Every melodic curve, rising or falling, results from the sequence of two tonemes on two juxtaposed vowels, prolonged vowels being interpreted as sequences of homogeneous vowels. c) In Dida, tones are stable at the level of lexemes.
tn.cite: Masson, Denis. 1992. Esquisse phonologique du dida de Yocoboué. In I. Egner (ed.), Esquisses phonologiques de trois langues ivoiriennes, 1-56. Abidjan: ILA/SIL; Paris: ACCT.
tn.note: Three level tones H/M/L, one per syllable; rising/falling contours are two tonemes on vowel sequences (long vowels = two vowels). A word-initial 'accent tonique' is only an unverified hypothesis.
